expected_segments: A safe interaction needs both a rule and an understanding of how people are moving. Establish your duty first, then keep observing. Having priority never makes a collision acceptable.

In this chapter M04-L01 · Decide who goes first M04-L02 · Turn with a complete picture M04-L03 · Crossings belong to people M04-L04 · Choose a safe path through a roundabout M04-R · Review and self-assessment Answers and review guidance Official references This material is a learning aid to help you understand Swedish driving theory. It is not an official source and cannot replace official information from Trafikverket and Transportstyrelsen. Always consult their current guidance and the applicable rules.
Your goal: Explain junction decisions using priority instructions and right-hand priority, and recognise special situations.

Requirements. Where two vehicle paths cross, the general rule is to yield to a vehicle approaching from your right, except where another applicable rule or instruction determines the relationship. Road width, familiarity or the fact that you are travelling straight does not by itself establish priority. Right-hand priority can apply at a three-way junction or within a parking area. Right-hand priority · Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §18
Priority and junction instructions Independent examples: A29 variants show different branch layouts. Read thick and thin roads on each T15 panel; do not assume an approach orientation.
The junction ahead is governed by the right-hand priority rule. Do not assume the broader road has priority. Black cross inside a warning triangle.
Junction with right-hand priority. Black cross inside a warning triangle.
Continue the learning

Traffic joining from the connecting roads must yield or stop. Match the diagram to the actual junction; it does not remove your duty of care. Thick straight road with a thin road joining from each side at right angles.
Junction with yielding side roads. Thick straight road with a thin road joining from each side at right angles.

Traffic joining from the connecting roads must yield or stop. Match the diagram to the actual junction; it does not remove your duty of care. Thick vertical road with a thin perpendicular branch to the left.
Junction with yielding side roads. Thick vertical road with a thin perpendicular branch to the left.

Traffic joining from the connecting roads must yield or stop. Match the diagram to the actual junction; it does not remove your duty of care. Thick vertical road with a thin perpendicular branch to the right.
Junction with yielding side roads. Thick vertical road with a thin perpendicular branch to the right.
Continue the learning
A priority road begins or continues. Still check the actual junction, controls and other road users. Yellow diamond inside a white border.
Priority road. Yellow diamond inside a white border.
The priority-road designation ends. Assess the rules at the next junction afresh. Priority-road diamond crossed by a black diagonal band.
End of priority road. Priority-road diamond crossed by a black diagonal band.
Drivers on every approach to the junction have a yielding duty. Text Flervägsväjning on yellow.
All approaches give way. Text Flervägsväjning on yellow.
Drivers on every approach to the junction have a stopping duty. Text Flervägsstopp on red.
All approaches stop. Text Flervägsstopp on red.
Continue the learning
Traffic on the thin-line roads yields to traffic on the thick-line road. Follow the actual road layout shown. Thick road connects the top and right edges; thin branches extend down and left.
Priority-road layout at the junction. Thick road connects the top and right edges; thin branches extend down and left.
Traffic on the thin-line roads yields to traffic on the thick-line road. Follow the actual road layout shown. Thick road connects the top and left edges; thin branches extend down and right.
Priority-road layout at the junction. Thick road connects the top and left edges; thin branches extend down and right.

Different duties apply when entering a road from premises, a car park, fuel station, similar roadside area, path or similar exit, or from terrain, a pedestrian street, walking-speed area or cycle street. After crossing a footway or cycle path to enter a road, the exit provision also matters. Do not decide solely from a kerb's appearance; identify the actual layout. Joining a priority road without an acceleration lane generally requires yielding, subject to the provision for joining without changing lane. Roundabout entry has its own duty. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§21–23

To yield, show your intention by reducing speed or stopping in good time. Only continue when the other road user's position, distance and speed allow movement without danger or obstruction. A stop duty requires a complete stop even if the road appears empty. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§5 and 19
Yielding and stopping Signs and markings are labelled counterparts. The separate stopping-point illustration shows how the line relates to the car.
Yield to vehicles on the crossing road or route. With a distance or stop-ahead panel, this can instead be advance information. Inverted triangular give-way sign.
Give way. Inverted triangular give-way sign.
Make a complete stop before entering the crossing road, route or track area. Use the stop line; without one, apply the prescribed stopping position. Red octagon bearing STOP.
Stop. Red octagon bearing STOP.
This identifies where to stop when a sign or signal requires it. The line alone does not create a universal stop duty. Wide transverse white stop line.
Stop line. Wide transverse white stop line.
Continue the learning
This identifies the line drivers should not pass while yielding. Row of white give-way triangles.
Give-way line. Row of white give-way triangles.

Learning approach. Ask three questions: What controls this conflict? Whose path crosses mine? Can I make the decision early enough that the other person understands it? Do not wave someone into a situation you cannot assess for them.
Ordinary junction or exit?
Ordinary junction: no signs, signals or special rule apply. The yellow car approaches from the teal driver’s right. Road width alone does not determine priority.
Driveway exit: the teal car is entering across the footway. Identify the exit duty before choosing a gap.
Worked decision. You approach from a driveway on the right of a car travelling along the road. You yield under the exit rule. Being on the other driver's right does not displace that duty.
Driving on a priority road B4
Driving on a priority road: B4 is after the junction on the right verge. B1 controls the side-road approach. Continue observing; priority does not make a collision acceptable.
Where a stop is required
Stop duty: the teal car approaches the stop line. A complete stop is required at the line. This detail shows the stopping point, not the whole junction.
Check your understanding
Knowledge check. You drive straight on a broad road and another car approaches from the right on a narrower ordinary road. No signs, signals or special rule apply. Who yields?
Remember: Determine the applicable rule before judging the available gap.
Your goal: Plan observation, signalling, position and margins for turns and lane changes.

Requirements. Before a turn, check that it will not obstruct oncoming traffic or traffic on the road you are entering. Pay attention to people travelling in the same direction, including those behind you. Position early: normally the right-hand lane for a right turn and the left-hand lane for a left turn where multiple approach lanes exist, subject to applicable signs, markings and space provisions. On a two-way road, a left turn is normally prepared near the road centre; on a one-way carriageway, near the left edge. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§24–29
Choose a permitted direction Prohibitions, mandatory directions, one-way signs and lane arrows are separate sets. They are not all present at one fictional junction. Prohibited movements
The depicted turn is prohibited at the relevant junction. A length panel can extend the restriction across several junctions. Left-turn arrow crossed out.
Prohibited turn. Left-turn arrow crossed out.
Continue the learning
The depicted turn is prohibited at the relevant junction. A length panel can extend the restriction across several junctions. Right-turn arrow crossed out.
Prohibited turn. Right-turn arrow crossed out.
A U-turn is prohibited at the relevant junction or location. Read any panel extending the restriction. U-turn arrow crossed out.
No U-turn. U-turn arrow crossed out.
Mandatory directions
Travel only in a direction shown by the arrow or arrows. Arrow points left.
Mandatory direction. Arrow points left.
Travel only in a direction shown by the arrow or arrows. Arrow points right.
Mandatory direction. Arrow points right.
Continue the learning
Travel only in a direction shown by the arrow or arrows. Arrow points straight ahead.
Mandatory direction. Arrow points straight ahead.
Travel only in a direction shown by the arrow or arrows. Arrows permit straight ahead or left.
Mandatory direction. Arrows permit straight ahead or left.
Travel only in a direction shown by the arrow or arrows. Arrows permit straight ahead or right.
Mandatory direction. Arrows permit straight ahead or right.
Travel only in a direction shown by the arrow or arrows. Arrows permit left or right.
Mandatory direction. Arrows permit left or right.
One-way road
Vehicle traffic travels only in the arrow's direction on this road. One-way arrow points right.
One-way traffic. One-way arrow points right.
Vehicle traffic travels only in the arrow's direction on this road. One-way arrow points straight ahead.
One-way traffic. One-way arrow points straight ahead.
Lane arrows

Choose the appropriate lane for the next junction. Where a continuous line bounds the lane, follow its arrow directions, subject to the specified reserved-lane exception. Examples of straight, branching and turning lane arrows.
Lane arrows. Examples of straight, branching and turning lane arrows.

For a lane change or significant sideways movement, signal clearly and in time, then check that the movement can be made without danger or unnecessary obstruction. The indicator announces an intention, not a claim on a gap. Drivers who notice another vehicle intending to join their lane must adjust speed to help; when two lanes merge into one, both drivers must adapt with mutual consideration. These duties work together. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§43–44 and 65–66
Changing and merging lanes Compare merging, lane increase, lane reduction and a lane-change arrow. Establish the actual road layout before deciding how to move.
Two lanes or carriageways join. Drivers must adapt with mutual consideration; this is not an instruction to force a gap. Two paths combine into one upward arrow.
Merge. Two paths combine into one upward arrow.
The number of lanes increases. Read the diagram for direction and any physical separation. An additional lane opens on the left.
Additional lane. An additional lane opens on the left.
The number of lanes decreases. Use the diagram to plan a safe change early. The left-hand lane merges into the remaining forward lane.
Lane reduction. The left-hand lane merges into the remaining forward lane.
Continue the learning
A lane change is needed promptly. Check that the manoeuvre can be made safely. White change-lane arrow bending sideways.
Change-lane arrow. White change-lane arrow bending sideways.

Learning approach. Read the path through the turn, not just the point at which you steer. Check the mirror view and the areas it does not cover. Look for a cyclist alongside before turning across their route. Recheck the receiving road, crossings and queue space. If the information changes, pause the manoeuvre rather than completing the original plan automatically.
Wait before steering

Safety advice · Wait with front wheels straight. When stopped waiting to turn left across oncoming traffic, keep your front wheels pointing straight ahead. Your indicator communicates the intended turn; your wheels do not need to point along that intended route while you wait. If a vehicle hits you from behind, front wheels already turned left can direct the pushed car into oncoming traffic. Keeping them straight helps reduce that risk, but cannot guarantee protection in a collision. Begin steering into the turn only when there is a safe opportunity to make it. New York DMV: waiting to turn left

Waiting is different from turning. Follow the positioning, signalling and observation requirements above. The wheel-position advice does not create permission to enter or block a junction, ignore a signal, or obstruct someone else's path. Continue observing oncoming traffic, the receiving road, crossings and vehicles behind you while waiting. Recheck the full path before moving.

Practice example. Sami is stopped in a suitable position, signalling left while oncoming cars pass. A passenger suggests turning the wheels left now to be ready. Sami keeps them straight: preparing the intention is different from starting the movement. Once the gap and receiving road permit a safe turn, he moves and steers into it. On rural roads, use M06-L01 to assess bends, crests and other risks before choosing a turning opportunity.
Changing lane or merging?
Lane change: two marked lanes continue. A signal communicates an intention; check for a safe opportunity before moving sideways.
Mutual merge: two lanes narrow into one. Both drivers adapt with mutual consideration.
Joining from an acceleration lane
Acceleration-lane join: a distinct joining lane meets the through lane. Adapt speed and join safely; do not force a gap.

This companion scene shows a distinct acceleration lane. Adapt speed to the traffic in the lane you intend to join and leave the acceleration lane as soon as this can be done without danger or unnecessary obstruction. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §23
Observe the complete turn
Right turn beside a cyclist: the cycling route and receiving road remain open. Check the cyclist’s movement before crossing the route. No movement arrow grants priority.

Worked decision. A driver signals to move right while a cyclist is beside the vehicle. The driver waits. Signalling earlier would have helped communication, but it would never have removed the need to ensure the cyclist's safety.
Check your understanding

Knowledge check. (1) Does a driver in the continuing lane have no responsibility when someone is merging? (2) You are stopped waiting to turn left across oncoming traffic. Which way should the front wheels point, why, and when should you start steering into the turn?
Remember: Communicate the plan, then confirm the space is still there.
Your goal: Distinguish pedestrian crossings, cycle passages and cycle crossings and apply the relevant duties.

Requirements. At an uncontrolled pedestrian crossing, yield to pedestrians who are on it or about to enter. Someone walking a bicycle is a pedestrian; someone riding one is not made a pedestrian merely by using the painted crossing. A person using a wheelchair at walking speed is covered by pedestrian rules. This distinction never removes the general duty to avoid danger. Pedestrian crossings · Wheelchair users · Traffic Regulation, chapter 1 §4 and chapter 3 §61
Recognise a pedestrian crossing The warning identifies an approach. B3 and M15 identify the crossing itself; the mirrored B3 artwork does not change the duty.
Prepare to encounter a pedestrian crossing. Identify the crossing itself and the controls that apply there. Pedestrian on crossing stripes inside a warning triangle.
Pedestrian crossing ahead. Pedestrian on crossing stripes inside a warning triangle.
Continue the learning
This identifies a pedestrian crossing. At an uncontrolled crossing, drivers yield to people who have entered or are about to enter. Pedestrian on crossing stripes within a white triangle on blue.
Pedestrian crossing. Pedestrian on crossing stripes within a white triangle on blue.

This identifies a pedestrian crossing. At an uncontrolled crossing, drivers yield to people who have entered or are about to enter. Mirrored pedestrian on crossing stripes within a white triangle on blue.
Pedestrian crossing. Mirrored pedestrian on crossing stripes within a white triangle on blue.
This marks the pedestrian crossing associated with B3. Identify whether it is signal-controlled before applying the crossing duties. Parallel white crossing stripes.
Pedestrian crossing marking. Parallel white crossing stripes.
Continue the learning
Situation
Driver's duty
Uncontrolled cycle passage, approaching without turning
Adapt speed so cyclists or class II moped riders already on the passage are not endangered. A rider coming from a cycle path generally has a yielding duty.
Uncontrolled cycle passage after your turn or roundabout exit
Travel slowly and allow riders on or about to enter the passage an opportunity to pass.
Cycle crossing (cykelöverfart)
Yield to cyclists and class II moped riders on it or about to enter it.

A cycle crossing has both markings and the cycle-crossing sign, together with a design that secures low vehicle speeds. Do not identify it only by painted blocks. Transportstyrelsen: cycle passages and crossings · Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§61–61a
Identify a cycle crossing Separately labelled components. M16 alone does not establish a cycle crossing; read the sign, markings and road design together.

This identifies a cycle crossing. Drivers yield to cyclists and class II moped riders on or about to enter it; riders must also consider approaching vehicles. Cyclist above a crossing in a blue square.
Cycle crossing. Cyclist above a crossing in a blue square.
This identifies the line drivers should not pass while yielding. Row of white give-way triangles.
Give-way line. Row of white give-way triangles.
Continue the learning

The blocks alone do not identify a cycle crossing. A cycle crossing also has B8 and the give-way marking M14; assess the controls and your movement. Two parallel rows of white blocks marking the sides of a cycle passage or crossing.
Cycle passage or cycle crossing marking. Two parallel rows of white blocks marking the sides of a cycle passage or crossing.

At a controlled pedestrian crossing, let people who entered correctly complete their passage even if your signal permits you to proceed. After turning across a controlled crossing, travel slowly and yield to pedestrians who have correctly entered or are about to enter. Corresponding duties apply to riders at controlled cycle passages. Keep the crossing clear when traffic ahead is queued. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§60–62

Signals and crossing duties Pedestrian indications and vehicle indications control different users. Printed pictures do not reproduce audible signals or guarantee conflict-free movement. Pedestrian signals
Do not begin crossing. If already crossing when it changes to red, continue to the other side or stop on a refuge where one exists. Red standing pedestrian; audible pulses are not reproduced.
Red pedestrian signal with slow audible pulses. Red standing pedestrian; audible pulses are not reproduced.
Continue the learning
Pedestrians may begin crossing. The still image does not reproduce the audible pulse pattern. Green walking pedestrian; audible pulses are not reproduced.
Green pedestrian signal with fast audible pulses. Green walking pedestrian; audible pulses are not reproduced.
Vehicle signals
Stop before the stop line or, if none, before the signal. An outline arrow limits the indication to the direction shown. Red left arrow, red full lamp and red bicycle signal examples.
Red vehicle signal. Red left arrow, red full lamp and red bicycle signal examples.

You may proceed subject to the remaining traffic duties. A green arrow applies to its direction, including when another signal indication appears simultaneously. Green arrow, green full lamp and green bicycle signal examples.
Green vehicle signal. Green arrow, green full lamp and green bicycle signal examples.
Two different crossing situations
Uncontrolled pedestrian crossing: a person is about to enter. The B3 sign and zebra marking identify this separate example.
Uncontrolled cycle passage approached without turning: M16 blocks mark the passage. There is no B8 cycle-crossing sign in this example.
The official artwork in each white reference card identifies the illustrated control or marking; it is not a new roadside sign assembly.
Identify the crossing and your movement
Cycle crossing: B8, the crossing markings and the raised treatment distinguish this example. Surface colour alone does not determine the duty.
Passage after a roundabout exit: the cyclist is approaching the marked passage on the receiving road. The exit movement matters to the driver’s duty.

Worked decision. You leave a roundabout and reach an uncontrolled cycle passage. A cyclist is about to enter. You slow and give the rider an opportunity to pass; applying only the straight-ahead passage rule would miss the significance of your exit.
Check your understanding
Knowledge check. Is every cycle passage a cycle crossing with the same yielding duty?
Remember: Expect a person to continue moving while you are interpreting the layout.
Your goal: Describe an approach, entry and exit plan that accounts for priority, lanes, signalling and nearby crossings.

Requirements. Travel anticlockwise and yield on entry to vehicles already circulating. Choose an appropriate lane for the onward route and obey signs and markings. There is no general requirement to signal solely for entering; signal lane changes and significant sideways movements, and signal right when leaving. Any lane change must be safe and must not create unnecessary obstruction. Transportstyrelsen: roundabout guide · Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§13, 22, 43 and 65–66
Roundabout instructions Approach warning, circulation direction, yielding, lane guidance and island marker are distinct instructions. Read the actual combination on the road.
Prepare for a roundabout and identify the entry instructions before reaching it. Circulating arrows inside a warning triangle.
Roundabout ahead. Circulating arrows inside a warning triangle.
Continue the learning
Follow the roundabout circulation. Identify the yielding instruction at the entry separately. Three white arrows circulate anticlockwise on blue.
Roundabout. Three white arrows circulate anticlockwise on blue.
Yield to vehicles on the crossing road or route. With a distance or stop-ahead panel, this can instead be advance information. Inverted triangular give-way sign.
Give way. Inverted triangular give-way sign.

On the approach to a roundabout, this marking helps you choose a suitable lane for the next junction and your onward route. Its layout is adapted to the location. Lane arrow with a roundabout diagram and several onward directions.
Roundabout lane arrow. Lane arrow with a roundabout diagram and several onward directions.
This identifies the centre around which vehicles circulate in the roundabout. A horizontal blue board bears successive white arrows pointing right.
Roundabout centre marker. A horizontal blue board bears successive white arrows pointing right.
Continue the learning

Learning approach. Read the layout before reaching the yield point. Reduce speed enough to judge circulating traffic and the available space. Observe crossings on the approach as separate conflicts. Inside, hold your intended path and continue checking nearby vehicles. A large vehicle may need more room than its apparent lane width suggests. Roundabout guide

Plan the exit early. Moving from an inner lane across an outer lane is a lane change, even though you call the whole movement “leaving the roundabout.” Do not assume a vehicle beside you will leave at the same exit. If the exit cannot be taken safely, continue as the layout allows and re-plan. On leaving, check the crossing area again; the duties in M04-L03 still apply. Roundabout guide · Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§60–62
Entry and circulation are separate decisions
Approach: B1 and D3 identify the entry instructions. The teal car approaches the yield point while the yellow car circulates anticlockwise.
Circulation: two lanes surround the island. The teal car in the inner lane and yellow car in the outer lane need separate space; the inner lane confers no exit priority.

Worked decision. Your desired exit is approaching, but a car is alongside in the outer lane. You do not cut across it. You preserve a safe path and choose another opportunity consistent with the lane markings. Recovering the route is secondary to avoiding a conflict.
Check the receiving road
Exit: the teal car approaches a cycle passage. Signal right when leaving and check the passage as a separate conflict.
Check your understanding
Knowledge check. Does a left signal give you permission to cross a neighbouring lane?
Remember: Entry, circulation, lane changes, exit and crossings are separate decisions within one journey.
Scenario: Leave a car park, turn left, pass a cycle crossing and enter a two-lane roundabout.
1. Leaving a car park. Describe the duty and the observations needed before entering the road.
2. Preparing a left turn on a two-way road. Identify the vehicles and paths you need to observe.
State each duty before choosing a gap.
Crossing and entry details
3. Approaching a raised cycle crossing. Read the official B8 sign and the markings before explaining the duty.
4. Entry detail. This companion image shows a single-lane entry; use the separate two-lane view for the written scenario’s lane decisions.
Use the two-lane companion view on the next page for the final part of the written scenario.
Plan the two-lane section
Two-lane companion view for the written scenario. Identify nearby vehicles and explain how you would plan a lane change and exit. No route is selected.
State each duty before choosing a gap.
Keep a practice record
Which conflict would be hardest to observe while also controlling the car? Record the consequence of noticing it late and arrange targeted supervised practice. Syllabus self-assessment, chapter 3 §3
